data.heading: Visiting the mandir: what to expect
data.body:
If you've never visited a Hindu temple, you're very welcome at [Mandir Name]. Here's what to expect.

When you arrive, you'll be asked to remove your shoes before entering. There are racks near the entrance. [Add your dress guidance here.]

Inside, you'll see the shrine or shrines of [Presiding Deity / Deities]. Devotees come for darshan, which means seeing and being seen by the deity. You're welcome to stand quietly and observe.

Aarti is a good time to visit. Lamps are waved before the deities while prayers and songs are sung. At the end, the flame is often brought around and people pass their hands over it. You can join in or simply watch.

After aarti, prasad is often shared. It's a blessed offering of food, and visitors are welcome to accept it.

Please ask before taking photos. [Add your photo policy.]

If you'd like a guided visit, contact the office and we'll be happy to arrange one.

data.heading: Celebrating festivals at the mandir
data.body:
Festivals are among the most joyful times at [Mandir Name]. The mandir fills with families, music, color and food.

Hindu festivals follow a lunar calendar, so their dates change each year. We post confirmed dates and times on our events page and share them by [email / social media].

Diwali, the festival of lights, is one of the busiest times of the year. Navaratri brings nine nights of worship and celebration. [Add other festivals your community celebrates.]

Each festival usually includes special pujas and aarti, and often bhajans, cultural programs and a community meal. [Describe what your mandir typically holds.]

Festivals rely on many volunteers. If you'd like to help with decorations, the kitchen or parking, sign up on our Seva page.

If you're coming for the first time during a festival, arrive early. The mandir can be very busy, and parking may be limited. [Add parking guidance.]

Everyone is welcome, including friends and neighbors who aren't Hindu. Come and celebrate with us.
